name: Irisglow
lede: Irisglow is a pale, faintly purple grey that Maerz and Paul recorded in 1930, and no other system in our library repeats it.

sections.title: A fashion-dictionary name
sections.body: Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* places Irisglow on plate 44, swatch B3, first recorded in 1928 [1]. A color this close would be filed by the ISCC-NBS system as a pale purple [1]. Its nearest named neighbor in our library is [[platinum-grey|Platinum Grey]], and the closest common color word is [[grey|Grey]] itself, under seven units away in CIEDE2000 [1]. It sits in our library's Neutrals family not far from [[ash]] and [[taupe]], though neither is a precise match [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within six units of Irisglow covers at least five percent of the canvas in 230 of our 23,781 paintings, 0.97 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 131 [2]. That ranks it ahead of 63 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 31 of 1,674 paintings, at 1.9 percent of that decade's paintings, 2.3 times the archive's overall rate, and it most often plays a light, in 46 percent of its 131 appearances [2].

Claude Monet is its most devoted painter, in four of his 50 paintings here, six times the rate of the museums those works come from [2]. The earliest matching painting dates to 1119, 811 years before Maerz and Paul recorded the name in 1930 — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof the color existed as a dye that early, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
